items.stem: If 3 coins are tossed 80 times, the expected frequency of exactly 2 heads under fairness is:
items.explanation: For three fair coins, P(exactly two heads)=C(3,2)(1/2)³=3/8. Across 80 repetitions, the expected frequency is 80×3/8=30.

items.stem: The chi-square test statistic must be computed from:
items.explanation: The Pearson chi-square statistic is Σ(Oᵢ−Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ, where Oᵢ and Eᵢ are the observed and expected frequencies. It is computed from frequency counts, not percentages or ranks.

items.stem: In a chi-square test, Σ(Oᵢ − Eᵢ) always equals:
items.explanation: When observed and expected frequencies refer to the same total, ΣOᵢ=ΣEᵢ. Subtracting gives Σ(Oᵢ−Eᵢ)=0.

items.explanation: A chi-square test of homogeneity or a test of equal proportions compares categorical frequency distributions across groups. Its statistic is based on observed and expected cell counts.

items.stem: When ties are present, the correct procedure is to:

items.explanation: When values are tied, assign each tied observation the average of the ranks they would have occupied. This is the standard midrank procedure.

items.explanation: Spearman's rho is Pearson's product-moment correlation calculated on the ranks rather than on the original measurements.

items.explanation: Kendall's tau compares all pairs of observations and is based on the numbers of concordant and discordant pairs.

items.explanation: The largest Σd² occurs when ranks are completely reversed. Its value is n(n²−1)/3; for n=10 this is 10×99/3=330.

items.stem: Rank correlation is preferred to Pearson’s r when:
options: the relationship is monotone but non-linear
items.explanation: Rank correlation is appropriate when the association is monotone but need not be linear, or when ordinal ranks are more meaningful than raw measurements.

items.explanation: For two independent normal samples, the ratio of their sample variances (after scaling by the population variances under the null) follows an F distribution.

items.stem: Testing a single population variance against a specified value uses:
items.explanation: Under normality, (n−1)S²/σ₀² follows χ² with n−1 degrees of freedom under the null hypothesis about one population variance.

items.stem: Comparing the means of five groups simultaneously uses:
items.explanation: One-way ANOVA compares several group means simultaneously. The ratio of between-group to within-group mean squares is tested using an F statistic.

items.stem: The nonparametric alternative to the two-independent-sample t test is:
items.explanation: The Mann–Whitney U test is the rank-based alternative to the two-independent-sample t test.

items.stem: The nonparametric alternative to oneway ANOVA is:
items.explanation: The Kruskal–Wallis test is the rank-based alternative to one-way ANOVA for comparing several independent groups.

items.stem: For paired observations, the appropriate parametric test is:
items.explanation: For paired measurements, form the within-pair differences and apply the one-sample t test to those differences.

items.explanation: As the degrees of freedom grow, the t distribution approaches the standard normal distribution.

items.stem: The expected value of U under H₀ is:
items.explanation: Under the null hypothesis that the two populations have the same continuous distribution, E(U)=n₁n₂/2.

items.stem: The variance of U under H₀ is:
items.explanation: Without ties, Var(U)=n₁n₂(n₁+n₂+1)/12. This is the null variance used in the normal approximation.

items.stem: In the Mann–Whitney test, ties are handled by:
items.explanation: Tied observations receive average ranks in the pooled ranking. The variance calculation is then adjusted for ties.

items.stem: The sum of all ranks in a pooled sample of size N is:
items.explanation: The ranks in a pooled sample of size N are 1,…,N. Their sum is N(N+1)/2.

items.stem: The nonparametric analogue of the paired t test is:
items.explanation: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test uses the signs and ranks of paired differences and is the nonparametric analogue of the paired t test.

items.stem: The Kruskal–Wallis test is used for:
items.explanation: The Kruskal–Wallis test compares three or more independent groups using pooled ranks.
